Like I said, I mean we got a lot of people playing a lot of positions. So, um you know, just seeing these young guys kind of kind of learn, you know, as they go, it kind of reminds me like as myself when I was a younger guy, too, just kind of learn different spots. Um, and then kind of like seeing like the growing areas and areas for growth and, you know, come back the next day and you can see the difference in in the growth from each guys. So, it's pretty cool to see. >> New faces, a new staff. Does it feel kind of like a new organization in a sense? >> Uh, yeah, it does actually. Uh, I mean, we watched some clips from practice yesterday in a team meeting. It's like, wow. It's almost like >> not embarrassing in a way, but it's like we're I mean, we're we're so we're so much better now um than looking at certain things from last year. How would you describe the culture that Kubak is setting? >> Um, I think he's bringing a lot out of the players, which is cool to see. Um, you know, one thing he's encouraged us is to show our personalities out there on the field. Uh, so just, you know, bringing bringing energy from from that from that side of things that, um, he's put he puts a lot of trust in us and, you know, I think, you know, as a as a group, we appreciate that. >> Do you have >> What's that? >> What type of personality do you show in the DB room? I think I think you should answer that question. >> This is a question for 10, not for love. [laughter] >> Not for who? >> Love. >> Uh, what type of personality do I show? Um, I don't know. I feel like I'm direct, man. I got a direct way of communication to the whole group. Um, I don't know. I guess I'm just myself. >> What What do you see, Eric? >> I don't I don't know. I'm not [laughter] Next question. >> What have you seen from his masters this off season? >> Oh man, Zeke came in making plays. Um, I mean, even in OTAAS and stuff, just seeing seeing him step up and just I feel like he just had an understanding. Um, even just technique-wise, like he he he's true to his technique. He's always been true to his technique ever since he, you know, stepped in here. Um, and it hasn't been a drop off, so you know, it's been cool to see. Yeah, I mean he's he's been on the field now, too. And um he's been shopping. I mean, he's he's been making plays on the ball um every time he's out there. >> What's been the biggest differences so far in Rob Leonard's scheme? >> I don't want to talk too much scheme. >> Well, Robert, what's what has he brought to this team now that he's gone from defensive line to defensive coordinator? >> Yeah. Um, I mean, as you know, Rob Rob's a defensive line guy, but, uh, seeing him just just be in different rooms, whether it be the linebacker room or DB room or Dline room, whatever. Um, you know, he he's kind of had like a piece in everything. So, um, you know, that's that's been impressive to see. I mean, just the guys that the the coaches that he has in those positions, whether it be Trav or or Matt or, you know, Rell or something. Um, just letting those guys coach and I think as each group continues to get better, um, and get strong and and find those leaders, uh, I think it all kind of falls under the same roof, uh, which Rob is building. So, it's it's cool. >> We've seen Terron Johnson play a pretty versatile role in this secondary. as a veteran coming into, you know, a new team like this, how important is it for a guy like him to be buying into that role and doing stuff that's new for him? >> Uh, I mean, it's really important. I mean, we brought him here for a reason. You know what I'm saying? He's played a lot of good football over his career. Uh, so I mean, he'll he'll help us a whole lot. >> All right. Thanks, Jeremy. >> Thank you guys. Appreciate it.

title: One-on-one with right tackle Jalen Travis & defensive end Laiatu Latu | The Colts Show
text: I have Barney at the crib. I have you know little bags at the crib that I'll hit with when I'm bored or [music] something like that. But definitely when I'm if I'm hitting the corner like this has been since like college. If I'm hitting the corner I'll just I'll dip the shoulder or I'll like you know I'll I'll do a little swim move around it just a little bit you know. >> I have to laugh at walking into his kitchen. You you dip that shoulder a little bit. You know yeah. >> Then I'm spilling stuff everywhere all over it. >> It is my pleasure here to be welcomed on the Colt Show presented by Microsoft Surface Co-pilot plus PC by Colt's offensive lineman Jaylen Travis. Jaylen this is after the first training camp practice of 2026. How does it feel just being back out there getting back to football? >> It feels great getting back in the rhythm of things getting back with the guys. I'm excited you know to to just be around such a special group and you know to really work towards something that you know we think can be truly great. >> What you you got in a little bit last year. You started four games I believe it was. Got in against Jacksonville. What did you take away from just that little stretch of of football you got to play being the starter at right tackle? >> Yeah I think consistency is key you know and I think that was was huge for me to to prove to both you know myself and the organization that you know I can be a guy that can step up in that spot and and play consistently against some of the better ends in the league and the teams that we played you know down that stretch you know really exemplified that for sure. >> I mean your first game as a starter at right tackle you're playing the Seahawks. >> Yep. >> Won the Super Bowl based on having the best defense in the NFL and then you get the Texans to end the season and who >> No. >> had also the best defense in the NFL. I don't know how you differentiate those two. What did you learn from playing like DeMarcus Lawrence, Will Anderson, Trayvon Walker kind of that gauntlet of edge guys down the stretch there? >> Yeah I mean you just got to really focus on your own technique. You know these guys are are really good players get paid a lot of money to beat you. But you know I know and something that I learned throughout you know the course of those games like if I do what I need to do you know I'm very hard to beat and you know you're never going to have a perfect game um, and you're going to have those up and down plays, but making sure that you're able to respond against some of those better players is key. >> That you you mentioned not having a perfect game. That's something I've talked with coach Sparano about on occasion is like, you know, hey, it's it it's impossible to throw a perfect game, right? Like the in baseball it happens once every 10 years. For you as a an offensive lineman though, what mentality do you have to have to try to throw that perfect game? And then if if you can't, how do you respond to maybe, you know, one play where you get beat, um, so it doesn't turn into two or three? >> Yeah, you just have to trust your preparation. I think at the end of the day, you know, if you, you know, bust your tail Monday through Saturday, um, Sunday becomes fun. And you're able to just trust your technique, trust your prep. Um, and when those plays do come where you get beat or you know, isn't the best play, um, just being able to come back to the plate and keep swinging, um, because games are long and it's all games often right away and, you know, the team is able to come back after some of those plays more consistently, um, is typically the team that wins. >> For for you, um, you barely played with Daniel Jones last year. I know you got in a little bit in the Miami game toward the end of it when he was in. You were in as the sixth offensive lineman on occasion, but you know, he gets hurt against Jacksonville and then later in the second quarter you come in for Brighton Smith who got hurt in that game. Um, just being back out there with Daniel today, what sort of stands out about the way that he commands this offense? >> Yeah, I mean, consistent and clear communication is something that we appreciate on the offensive line and, you know, Daniel is the true captain of that ship and he makes sure that, you know, we're all on the same page, um, everything from protections to checks to huddle communication. And that's something that I truly appreciate because it removes, especially the young player, any ambiguity, um, you know, when we're out there on the field. So, you know, Daniel is huge when it comes to that. >> I mean, that just has to give you kind of a clear mind of like, you know how to execute your assignment because he's he's commanding that. >> Absolutely. And it was fascinating last year coming in under a guy like Philip Rivers and then, you know, with with with some of that communication and then, you know, having a guy with Daniel where there's no drop off, um, has been awesome for me definitely as a young player. >> I mean, you I don't know if you've ever looked at these things where it's like, this guy played with this guy who played with this guy. Like, you're like one step away from like LaDainian Tomlinson. For [laughter] having played with Philip Rivers last year. And like, you know, we're going to look back in like 30 years and it's, you know, you'll have a teammate toward the end of your career who'll be like, man, this guy played with Jalen Travis who played with Philip Rivers. >> That's crazy. >> What What did you learn from Phil last year though? >> I think a lot of it was preparation. You know, I had the privilege of sitting next to him in the team the team meeting room, which was awesome just to see the diligence in which he approaches the game, the things that he's looking for, especially on the offensive line, you know, coming in with a guy like that on the road at Seattle for my first start and his first start back. But just seeing how fluid in communication that he had, you know, really inspired me for sure. >> What What did What stands out to you just about the way that you're coached in that offensive line room? Because like, when I've talked to Coach Sparano, he says he coaches everyone in that room the same, whether you are the starter and you're a Quenton Nelson and you're an eight-time Pro Bowler, or you're an undrafted free agent trying to make the team. How did that level of coaching prepare you to step in and and be the best version of yourself as quickly as possible? >> You know, it was awesome. I think a guy who was in my spot, you know, with the twos last year, you know, Coach Sparano took the time with all of us to watch the film, to get into the weeds of our scout team film, him and Chris Watt. And for me, that was awesome and really aided my development to know that, you know, every single play that I have in practice is still going to be coached up to the to the best. And that was something that I think helped me come in with four or five games left in the season and perform the way I did. >> Uh in your media on Tuesday, you said something aspirational. You talked about decreasing body fat and increasing muscle mass this off season. Think we all would like to do that. What did you do this off season to kind of intentionally get yourself ready for the grind of playing 70-80 snaps a game? >> Yeah, uh I think a lot of it was like, okay, how do I take care of my body? What is my routine and my process look like? And I had the privilege of, you know, not, you know, playing a huge role last year early on, so I could really work on that process behind the scenes. And I think this year going into the season where expectations are high, making sure that I was really able to dial in on my process, everything from, you know, my meals to my training regimens, getting a little bit more unique with, you know, Pilates and you know, I even took a salsa class this offseason to work on some of my footwork. So, you know, I'm definitely trying to push the ends of of where the margins are um to try to figure out what the best version of Jaylen can be on the field. >> Tell me about the first time you walked into that salsa class. >> Oh. >> [laughter] >> My instructor was like 5 ft, and she ended up being my partner for the day. >> Um but it was like, all right, okay, like let's let's work with it. All right. Uh you know, it was very rough the first class, but, you know, by the end of it, like I was pretty confident in my abilities. Still got some, you know, little stiff hips here and there, but um it was definitely a dope experience. >> Okay, so you're ready to be on Dancing with the Stars then? >> Soon enough. >> That's a good segue into I I wanted to ask you about playing basketball growing up cuz you played AAU with Chet Holmgren and Jalen Suggs. >> Yeah. >> Um what did what did just like playing basketball do for you? And I guess like if you're talking to kids who are trying to get into sports, >> Right. >> like you you were never specialized in one thing. How did that all just maybe benefit you to get you where you are now? >> Yeah, I think the biggest thing with basketball is that it forces you to be a versatile player. Um you're never just expected to do one thing. But no one rarely is ever just a shooter or just a big man who can post up on one side of the block. You know, basketball forces you to guard every position, or at least how we played it, forces you to post up on different sides of the block, you know, mid-range game, you know, outside game. And for me, that really helped my athleticism to come on the football field and really be able to just shine, especially putting on more strength and more body mass. Um you know, allowed me to excel in those areas. And I think for youth growing up, it's extremely important I think to play multiple sports and really expose your body to these different, you know, modes of athleticism that you're going to have to have. So, when you do choose to specialize later on in your career, um your exposure to these different angles and body positions is is not, you know, unfamiliar. >> I love that. Um did anyone ever out-rebound you guys? >> No. No. No. I took pride in that. Uh I was the enforcer in high school, you smooth little 12 and 12 average. So, like I'll I'll take that. >> Okay, you had a double-double every game. Yeah. >> Come on. >> Okay, I mean I If you got you you and Chet out there >> Right. Like man, come on. Crazy. We had that AAU team was was pretty stacked. I think we had seven or eight guys that were going division one for either football or basketball. So, um those were those were the good times. >> And this is Minneapolis. >> Just >> Through and through. >> Okay, that's amazing. >> Um speaking of Minneapolis, you uh this off-season you you established the Nexus Now Foundation. which uh and you also held a leadership summit in Minneapolis. >> Uh tell me a little bit about that. Like what was your motivation behind doing this? What what's the purpose of this foundation and and the impact you're trying to make with it? >> Yeah, so the view behind Nexus Now is one investing in the leaders of tomorrow today. So, how can we give those students who are doing all the right things, but have outgrown their environments, whether it's because of resources, opportunities, um spaces and places that they yet don't know exist. How can we provide some of those, you know, spaces and resources and people and mentors to help them really plant the seed of the vision that they truly can become. Um so, we had the first iteration of, you know, what we hope will grow this summer in the Travis Leadership Summit. So, you know, taking high school captains and high school leaders from, you know, our men's and women's basketball and football programs from across the metro Minneapolis, um and bringing them together for a day full of seminars, um to which they went through professional leadership, you know, discussions, uh financial literacy, ACT and SAT prep. And then towards the end of the day, we brought in an organization called Athletes Committed to Educating Students with about 80 middle schoolers. So, for our high schoolers who are learning about leadership throughout the day, had an opportunity to practice some of that in real time with our middle schoolers on the field in a NFL style, you know, combine format. >> I mean, is is this something you always wanted to do to like use your platform to give back in in a very specific and I think a very impactful way? >> Absolutely. I think, you know, giving back in service is is a core part of my identity and I think it's really reflective of my purpose here. Um, you know, God-given. And I think for me when I talk about giving back, I wanted it to be something more reflective of my journey with some of the academic side, you know, the holistic picture to what a player can be, should be. And I wanted to make sure that even though it's not talked about as much, especially in aspirations that people have to make it professionally, that, you know, I'm able to provide a space where those discussions can be had and those examples, you know, can be made. >> Uh, kind of along those lines, Jaylen, I looked at your LinkedIn. It is impressive. I mean, the [laughter] amount of things you have on your LinkedIn and the amount of things you were involved in uh during your time at Princeton, you know, even now up to today. Um, how did how did you learn though at Princeton to balance all these other these things that you're doing and the impact you're making through them with working on your journey to get to where you are now, which is the starting right tackle in the NFL? >> 100%. Um, you know, it was never perfect and I think the highs and lows of an environment that's so demanding like Princeton, you really have to understand where your priorities are. And for me, you know, football was always going to be be a priority for me and that was something I was unwilling to sacrifice from. Um, and the dual part of that is both my academic and service life. And those were areas where I knew that would fill my cup in order to approach football with the diligence and the energy that I needed to. So, the more I was able to involve myself with giving back, with, you know, helping other people expose themselves to the realities of what a Princeton can be maybe in their future, really helped fill my cup and, you know, allows me to approach the game of football with a an energy and ambiance that maybe I wouldn't otherwise be able to. >> And it still continues today with like the what you're doing with the Nexus now then. It's kind of along those same lines, right? >> Absolutely. Absolutely. And I think, you know, I I was a little aggressive this off season with my team, you know, making sure that, you know, we're able to start using my platform earlier on in my career to make sure that, you know, that cup is filled for me. So, when the dog days of training camp get long, um I remember really the impact that I'm doing it for and the the kids are part of, you know, Nexus now and the Travis Leadership Summit who really glean to me for some of that inspiration. Um and it makes the sucky days a little bit less sucky. Um so, >> Okay, that is a great way to end it. Jaelan Travis thanks for time here on the pod. >> Thank you, JJ. Appreciate it. >> All right, back here on the Colts Show. It's my pleasure to be joined by defensive end Laiatu Latu. Uh Latu, we were just chatting before we kind of started here. I was like, your appearance on the media day podcast, you were like my favorite interview that we had out of like the 16 guys who came by the table. So, it's good to get you on a full length podcast here, man. >> Yeah, for sure. No, thank you for having me. >> Um so, we're we're kind of in in camp right now. Um what are you just sort of working on now in training camp that maybe you weren't able to get to in like year one and year two with the Colts? >> for this this year three going into year three for me, like it's just real I feel like less anxiety. Like I know my role. Um I'm really close with the guys in my room. So, like I know it's very like stress-free this year. Um not that it was anything bad before, but like, you know, just the nerves of coming into the league and stuff like that. But now it's like, you know, it just feels like home. I'm here like, you know, you know, me meandering around at home. I feel comfortable here, you know? >> How does that benefit you then of like, you're not necessarily worrying about like where you got to be at all times or like what you're doing at all times? You can just kind of it it's it's home. It's it's comfortable. How does that benefit you then going out here on the practice field? >> I mean, shoot, every like every day is like a flow. I get into a flow state like where, you know, I'm just boom boom here here and like in between times I can like, you know, I know what I have time for if I have time for ice bath, hot tub or like, you know, to do little things that like benefit me. Um which is which is dope. >> Can you Can you tell me like what is the difference for you when the pads are on versus the pads are off? Like this We're taping this after a non-padded practice. This episode's coming out a day I think it's day two of padded practices. What's the difference for you as a defensive end? >> Like in terms of on the field? >> Yeah, just like what does it feel like? >> Shoot, when I get the pads on, I mean it always takes me back to where I was a little kid putting pads on for the first time. But when I'm on the field like I don't know, it just it just feels like normal everything being on, everyone flowing around, you know, everyone with the helmets on and stuff. I mean >> Does it feel like football? >> It just feels like, you know, it feels like football. It feels like um >> [snorts] >> I've been doing this since like a 6 years old, 7 years old. So it just feels like a normal thing to me. It's like, all right, this is this is what we're doing every year. >> What What's that feeling like as a kid like putting on the pads for the first time and like then reflecting on it now you're in the NFL, you've had success in the NFL, you had three interceptions last year. I mean like you've had success but now reflecting on like that time you were six putting on the pads for the first time. >> It's just crazy how far like, you know, you've come from you know, just running around not knowing what to do, looking for people to hit, helmets like bigger than the rest of my body. Um but like reflecting on it now is just, you know, I got to always give thanks to God and just remember, you know, like there's so many people that have played football as a kid and like just to be able to be here among the greatest players, you know, in the world and just thinking back like, damn, I really was playing this as a kid not knowing like where I how far I'll come. >> What What's your why then? Like you get like I mean, camp is is a long it's a long process, it can be a grind. Uh the season is a grind, you're playing 17 games, all these snaps. Like what's the thing that you look back on and motivates you as your why >> Yeah. when you know things get tough or things get, you know, long and and the days are long like that? >> For me, what motivates me is it's always been my family, my mom, my brother, my my two little sisters. Um you know, those will always come first, but like when I'm out here like and you're here every day around everyone like it's definitely the guys. Like, everyone in my D-line group, you know, my whole defense, you know, I'll be seeing them from time to time. We have our little moments where we'll be la- laughing and stuff. You know, people on the offense, just like it's definitely the boys that that get me through. [clears throat] Like, cuz we're all going through it together. We're all, you know, experiencing everything together. Um you know, it's definitely them. >> How do you build that chemistry then? You know, you got a lot of new guys, new faces in that D-line room this year. How do you go about building that chemistry at this point of the year? >> I mean, I feel like, you know, and the Colts like do a great job of bringing in the right people. Um dudes who want to work, who want to get better. Um that are about ball and family and, you know, just being good people. Um I mean, it makes it easy when like you're being yourself and people like, you know, accept that. And like, you know, you see so many characters in in the NFL like and in the rooms like it's just it's it's very appreciative, you know. >> I want to go back to your mom a little bit. Like, you know, talking about, you know, playing football growing up and the journey you went on to get to this point now. Like, how important was your mom in supporting you and, you know, whether it's driving you to practice or working with you on whatever it might be. Like, just how important was, you know, has she been to you? >> Yeah, her role is like the most important in my life for sure because she's someone that's never left, you know, she's a single mom for pretty much all my life. Um Raising three four kids, including me, on her own, you know, going to work, making, you know, stuff work, taking us to school, practice, and all that. And um when I was actually uh medically retired, she played a big role in um helping me like get more second opinions and ultimately helping me get to UCLA just cuz of the doctors she reached out to. And the people she reached out to. So I mean, you know, moms are definitely the best and I definitely really appreciate her and love and love you, Mom. >> Moms are definitely the best. That's great. >> Um so you went to the Sack Summit. I know you've done that a couple of times, but um just tell me about that event. Like I know it's it's Max Crosby, Von Miller, Cam Jordan, three of the best pass rushers of all time put it on. Um tell me about the event. Like who's there outside of them? What do you do? What do you work on and who do you talk to at that summit? >> So I mean, it's dope because you get to meet everyone like that maybe you haven't met before. Like maybe haven't heard of. Um and really just get to pick each other's brains. Also like it's a you know, it's a big like bonding event too. Like where you know, you're just getting to know people and like then down the line you'll see them after a game or something and remember like the Sack Summit. But like ultimately we're there to you know, we're in the film room watching film with each other. Watching you know, Max, Cam, Von's tape. They're explaining certain things and we're watching little guy I don't mean that, but we're watching other guys um >> Like younger guys, right? >> yeah. I saw there were like college guys there too. Yeah, yeah. >> literally there's college guys there and stuff like that. >> Um so I mean, you know, it's just a dope feel to be around people at the same position and um really just learning off of um Von, Max, Cam. Really how to play certain situations and then taking it to the field. Um where we're doing like drills and stuff like that. So I mean, definitely a big like learning um like learning moment for sure. >> I saw something they posted it was Josh Allen being like you never know what's in someone else's brain. Like I mean you you got like these three great guys there, but I I wonder like if you could even pick something up from like a guy who went to Minnesota, you know, who's in college in Minnesota and he you know, pops up and you talking to him and you're like huh, you know, maybe that's interesting. Like there's so much knowledge there. >> Especially when you're on the field too and you're watching like someone hit like a rep and you notice them do something you're like, oh okay, let me ask him about that, you know? And if we do it, we do it even over here. Like, say you know, Buck hits him hits something, Key might hit something, you're like, "Oh, damn, like you know, what were you thinking right here?" Like, it's definitely like, you know, normal for us to do that. >> That level of communication, too. Like, just to to figure out that one thing. How many times do you have to rep it then to like actually get it into part of your your sort of toolbox? >> instantly as you're like questioning it, you're trying the movement, too. And still like they can look at you and see what's wrong, but like, you know, as soon as you're thinking about it, you think about how your body moves and how you can, you know, do the same thing in the in the certain situation. So, you know, all that's dope. >> Do you ever like practice pass rushing moves just like around the house? On like a doorway or something? >> Oh, definitely. I mean, I have I have Barney at the crib. I have a, you know, little bags at the crib that I'll hit with if I'm bored or something like that. But, definitely what I if I'm hitting the corner, like this has been since like college. If I'm hitting the corner, I'll just I'll dip the shoulder or I'll like, you know, I'll I'll do a little swim move around it just a little bit, you know? >> Oh, yeah. I'll tell you what. You walk into his kitchen, you you dip that shoulder a little bit, you know, yeah. over the kitchen. >> Um what do you do after a game? I think this is something that like not a lot of people see, right? We see what you do before a game a little bit. You We see obviously what you do during a game. But, like let's say it's a home game, it's 8:00, you're chilling. Like, what are you doing? >> Shoo, honestly, I probably if it was the away game, I'd probably watch some of the film on the plane. And then if I get home, I'll probably honestly hop on the game, see if my boys are on, chill. Um I'm into anime. So, like if I if I'm into an anime, I'll throw it on, watch it after the game, chill. Um really just low-key stuff, honestly. Yeah. >> You got to like decompress a little bit. >> Have to decompress. And being on the game with the boys is probably like one of the best That's how you decompress. >> Okay. That's great. Yeah. I mean, you can't like >> like what is that feeling in your body and like your mind? Cuz like the the mental and physical energy to play in an NFL game is something that no one understands unless you've ever done it before. >> Honestly, you're dead tired. Like um and you know, God willing you made it out the game without any injuries. But I mean, you're dead tired. You know, your mind has just been racing for like a couple hours straight. And you know, you're super sore, but like I don't know. You just want to be at home chilling, you know, people got family and stuff like that. Want to be kicking their feet up. Um I could just sit in my gaming chair and just listen to my boys joke around and stuff. So I mean, it's you know, I definitely look forward to that. >> And that's how you reset then for the rest of the week. Yeah, cuz then you lock right back in Monday when you get back into the facility. >> Um all right, I want to end on this. Uh give me your starting five of pregame essentials. What are things or routines or um just anything you have to do before you go out and play in an NFL game? >> I got to listen to music. >> What are you listening to? >> Ooh, that's a good question. I've like my music taste has gone everywhere over the years. So like really something that just makes me feel like like a serious moment or like it makes me feel like um like I don't know how to describe it. I just I love all kinds of music. That's but music is one. And then another Shoot. I don't know. I don't have many essentials before the game. >> Okay. I love it. Yeah. That's that's simple then. You don't really need a whole lot. >> Just music and then um really just being in there with the guys. Like coming here I thought I thought like you had to be so serious before a game. You know, and some people are like that, you know, and that's you know, understandable, but like it's it's it helps when like the nerves are relaxed in the locker room. >> Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. >> You know, we're talk I'm talking to Buck, you know, um Grove. We're just chill sitting there talking about the game or just you know, not just so like always like too intense. I I I like that, you >> That seems like that would probably have more of like a negative effect if you're just like so like you know, tense like that. Yeah. >> to be like that as a kid, but then over the years like you know, football became like a normal thing. So, it's like, "Okay, this you know, this is what I do." >> Yeah.
