So, >> did it let you play with a little bit more freedom out there knowing that you can take hits a little? >> Oh, yeah. Yeah. You know, I feel like honestly, nah, I feel like it's the same. Like I'm not really thinking about, you know, like even without pads, dudes still will tackle you. You know, it's not like it's not like they're going to just they're diving to make the plays as well. So, it is what it is at the end of the day, but um I feel like the pads on is just something you've been doing for a long time. >> Does it ramp up the energy obviously for the whole >> Yeah, I mean the the threes today, they went live, so you know, I mean they're they're they're hitting and tackling each other. So yeah, it definitely brings energy a little bit more. >> Kicking inside. Wallally's kicking inside this year against him. What have you seen from him after last year's injury? >> Yeah. Yeah. You know, Wall-E was a he was an outside corner in college and and even last year before he got hurt. >> So he's he's a guy that can cover really well and I feel like that helps me, you know, just go against a guy like that who's really quick, twitchy, and um similar to me. It makes me work a little bit more. But yeah, me uh Wallally's a great player. He doesn't, again, another guy that doesn't look like he's injured. He's he's quick, he's fast, he's he's making plays, and I know he's a guy that works on his craft a lot and he takes it serious. So, um to have him in there is huge. >> I know you don't see much of Sauce, but I mean, >> there's not a lot of match up like that in terms of his length and and wingspan. Just what what is that like and what kind of challenges? >> Yeah. No, I didn't been against Sauce a couple times, you Um, Saus is a guy, you know, he's really, really good player. Long and athletic, like you said, um, and he talks a little bit, so it's cool to, you know, talk with him, but no, great player. Um, him him and Mooney, they're bigger guys out there, but they also move well to be bigger. Um, so I feel like again, that's that's good for me to go against those type of guys each and every day. I mean, top corners in the league. I mean, if you have that at practice, I mean, the game will be a little bit easier. >> Would we I know we'd have a competition without Alec or even if Alec was out here. I know there's competition for that third wide receiver spot. What have you noticed from some of the guys um that you've been working with? Nick, um Ashton, some of those guys that are really kind of fighting for their jobs in this game. >> Uh I mean, we don't even look at it like that, but you know, um they they making plays. Treywell looks great. I mean, he's year 10 or 11 now, but he looks fresh. Uh Duelan looks great. Nick looks good. So, them dudes out there just making plays that come their way and um and just just keeping working. I mean, obviously, like you said, Alex not out there. Um we don't um so we just got to keep playing and practicing like we don't know when he's going to be back. Um obviously when he comes back we know what what he's going to do and be a great player and and get lots of targets but but for now those guys are making the plays that come their way.

title: Akheem Mesidor & Brenen Thompson On Their First Training Camp | LA Chargers
text: What's your uh first training camp going on so far? >> It's been cool. Um it's less taxing than it is in college. So, it's cool. Yeah, it's been all right. >> Has that been the biggest surprise so far for you or has it been? >> Yeah, you hear you like when you're in college, you hear a bunch of stories about different coaches and their approach when it comes to practice. Um some coaches like to go crazy and hit and do all the a bunch of stuff. Um Coach Harbaugh has been looking out and taking care of us, which is awesome. How excited are you getting pads on tomorrow? >> Very. Um I feel like I'm kind of being held back a little bit without pads. Obviously, you want to take care of each other, but um I like I harp on violence. Um that's how I play the game. So, it'll be exciting. >> How big will that be to kind of assess kind of where you're at this point? Pardon? >> How big will that be for yourself to evaluate like where you are at this point? >> Um I don't think it'll be huge. Uh I think I'm getting evaluated on what I'm doing right now, my work ethic, what I do pre-practice, postpractice, how I take care of my body, um the way I'm in my playbook. Um so this whole camp is really an assessment. I don't think tomorrow would be a huge jump. Let's just take it day by day. >> Can you say without pads just lining up across from guys like Joe Olaf, what you're able to take away from from that even without pads? Um they guys like that can get off the ball faster than you know guys in college do which I love. Um they're smart as well. So I'm very excited to go against both Joe Alt and Rashan every day. Very excited. talked to Khalil a few days ago and he sort of mentioned that he's pretty impressed with some of the detailed questions that you've asked him about various things whether it's sort of specific technique stuff or broad stuff about his career through training camp being on the field with him all day being in meeting rooms how have you sort of approached you know mining for that information from from Ko as you as you go through your first training camp [snorts] here >> it really happens on the fly I don't maybe I'll come I'll come into the building with a question in mind but most of them are just on the fly. So that we'll see something on film and I'll ask him a question right away or I'll ask Tulie a question. Um we'll be doing something on the field and it might feel a little awkward. Then I'll ask him on his perspective about whatever drill it was or however whatever technique it was. So it's awesome to have a guy like that in the room that I can just ask that's just available for me to ask questions whenever. Um I'll watch film and I've sent him clips and asked him questions. So like I'll text him whenever whatever it is. But um he's been a huge help. >> You mentioned it uh earlier, but how does that balance between uh sort of Yeah. like the holding back, right? Not wanting to injure anybody or injure yourself uh versus obviously wanting to get like the repetitions in and you know make that worthwhile. >> It's it's difficult. your first your first three to four steps are going to be full speed up to contact, but then you don't want to knock you don't want to keep knocking the O lineman back into the quarterback because you can you can't win a Super Bowl today, but you can damn sure lose it. Um, so it's it's difficult. You have to it's hard because it might develop bad habits cuz you have to stop at the level of the quarterback and then turn and run to the ball, which you don't want to do that in a game. In a game, you want to finish. So when we have Indie and and we have a quarterback that we have to finish on or a bag we have to finish on, you have to really really be intent in in in Indie, but um it's kind of a it's hard to find a balance, but once you find it, uh both sides of the ball can get good to work. >> Do you feel like you're learning a lot like technique-wise, stuff like that that that I mean it seemed like coming out everybody talked about how polished you were and ready to go you were, but how much more do you feel like you've learned since you've been here? I feel like it's really football. Football is simple. Dline is simple. It's really the fundamentals. Get off the ball, strike, pad level, full extension, violent hands, quick hands. Um, so just doing that every single day and just keep getting better at the fundamentals. It'll it'll be it'll you'll see a huge different in your huge difference in your game. I feel like where I've where I've learned a little bit was um in the film room, different coverages. So now I'm dropping now. So, um, learning coverages, different depth, different drops. Um, but most of it has been in the film room. On the football field, it's pretty simple. Just same fundamentals I've been doing since I was in college. >> How impactful has coach been for in that process just overall for you since? [snorts] >> Coach Coach has been cool. We don't meet with him often. Well, we'll be in we'll have our our D unit meeting which is like 15 minutes when it comes to drops and football and all that stuff. It's with uh Rooney. So CO has been cool. You whatever questions I have, I can ask him, but I've mainly been around Rooney. >> How do you think all of your physical tools have translate into this first uh you know, NFL camp? >> I think it's been good. Um I got a good get off. Um I got good hands. Uh I feel like I'm I'm very good fundamentally. So again, it's really simple. If you have the basic fundamentals and you have athletic ability to do it, you'll be fine. And I feel like it's translating it's translating well from college to this level. >> Similar to the last question, um all the playoff games and the important games you played, you know, recently, does that help you the level of competition and maybe a little bit of nervousness? You may or may not have. You think the high stakes games you played are kind of helping you or might help you in the future? >> I don't think so. >> No. >> No. Those those games I was prepared for those games before we before we ever before we ever stepped onto the field. >> Um I didn't >> I didn't develop my I guess >> I didn't develop that skill set >> in those games. It was practicing against our tackles every single day. Um being in you know intense situations. Coach Crystalall would have um crowd noise in the indoor. You can barely hear anything. We're going fast tempo. So, he created a kind of crazy environment before we ever got into a tough playoff environment. So, >> I was prepared for that before I even stepped onto the field. So, >> showed as a team. >> Yeah. So, we did we um we practiced a lot of that. And I'm not nervous stepping onto this field. Football is football. I truly believe in my athletic ability. Um, and I'm just here to play and practice, play, get better every single day. And, you know, we got two of the best tackles on this team as well. So, I'm grateful for that. And I'm able to get better and uh rush against them. >> For sure. >> How are y'all? >> Good. How are you? >> Awesome. I'm doing good. >> But, uh, what have you taken away here from the first five days of training camp? >> Oh, I think just the the, you know, anticipation of getting back to football after OTAAS and having some time off. Um, guys ready to go flying around. Uh, it's been fun. with your [clears throat] speed, how um how do you feel measuring? Do you do that like early on try to figure out who maybe the fastest guys are and kind of how your speed matches theirs? >> I don't think so. I think it's something that I just I've always done throughout my career is just I know my speed is pretty much unmatched when I step out on the field and that's something I take strong confidence in. Um so no matter what it is, um my coach and me personally, I'm just I'm flying to that spot or whatever it is and um yeah, just getting open. >> With Mike coming in, just how did you feel early and kind of where you feel like you're at right now? Um early was very very tough, very difficult. Um you know I'm coming from a system that's like hand signals, no huddle. Um and this is all huddle um 20 word you know from coming from the quarterback and so I'm just taking it day by day really diving into the playbook really um you know executing that part of it and then everything else will kind of slow down for me and take care of itself. >> We talked to Justin after the first day of camp and sort of asked him about you and his thoughts and was like he's going to be very good. That's what he said. What does it mean to sort of have that support from a player like Justin with his early career? >> I think it's awesome. Um, you know, obviously he's been a he's been a great quarterback, great leader to this this whole team, this whole club. Um, you know, I think that's that's a goal of every rookies when when they're coming in is to gain the trust of their their fellow teammates and coaches and um, you know, I'm working very hard every day to do that. >> Coach a little while ago, he said you're really versatile and willing to do a lot of different things. Is that something that you just try to kind of make your I guess stamp on your rookie season just being out there and doing what you can? >> Absolutely. Um, you know, I came here to to contribute to to make this team better. And so whether that's blocking, running, um, special teams, whatever that is, I'm going to put my best foot forward. How >> comfortable are you, you think, like returning punts, what he wants, and and kind of where you're at in that process right now? >> I think I'm very comfortable. Um, I think it's something I've, you know, you haven't seen a lot of in college, but it's something I always did every single week, um, whether prepping for a game. And so, um, I've always been prepared for that moment. And so, I'm just going to continue to to get better and focus on the little things with that. Um, and just continue to make strides. We've seen uh Justin take a couple deep shots to you here through the first first five days. Just >> how much chemistry needs to be built between a receiver and quarterback, especially somebody with pure speed to sort of figure out, you know, how much height to put on that ball, where to put it, how far in front of you can put it, like what is that process like as you go through this? >> Um, I definitely think it's all on me. Um, you know, showcasing that in practice so there's no switch up in the game and everything is super consistent so he can see, okay, this is where I need to put the ball. Obviously, Justin's a very talented player. um almost one-on-one. And so I think just for me and him gaining trust in me is okay, this needs to look the exact same every single time I run it. Um so he knows exactly where to put the football and so I think that's something that'll just come along with time. You >> mentioned adjusting to the different style of play calling. I mean what does that like adjustment sort of look like and maybe just overall who are like the players or coaches who really just helped you transition here? Um, I think it's something I I really, you know, put on myself to studying. Um, you know, and and being mature in that aspect and, you know, understanding that you can't really play football if you don't know what you're doing. Um, but it's been a it's been a big transition. I'm not going to lie. It's been huge. Um, you know, I'm used to one-word calls in college and now we're it's 20-word calls and you're having to really, you know, get the call from the quarterback and dissect which part belongs to you and then go out there and execute. Um, and so I think it's just I put a lot on myself to to study and know what I have each play. And um not only that, but also get the mental reps of the other, you know, 60 70 plays that all the other players are getting in in practice. And so um yeah, just making little little strides at a time. >> Just in terms of route running, um seeing a lot of that in the individual, just where you felt like you were coming in and where you feel like you are now and how much work is going into that, how comfortable you are, you know, do that without >> um yeah, I think there's there's a level to it. Um, you know, especially watching guys like Q and Lad and guys that have, you know, done it for a little bit and, um, I wouldn't say I'm necessarily too far behind. Um, I think it's just something that I continue need to get better at and continue to get more comfortable at. Um, definitely way more comfortable now than I was at OTAAS. I think that's just the nature of the game. Um, and coming with practice, but um, I'm nowhere near where I want to be right now. Um, I think if I was, we'd, you know, there'd be kind of issues. Um, so I think just continuing to to get with my coaches, to get with me, Daniel, get with coach Sanjay and and continuing to to watch the guys ahead of me and, you know, take pieces of their game and, you know, what can I really work on and get better at and um, yeah, I think running is something that is always in McDaniel's offense is huge. Um, you know, you always hear guys like like running off the ball, keep running off the ball. So that's something I've always done cuz I've always been fast. Um, so just picking apart the little things and, you know, making sure that the finer details and the smallest details, everything matters. and start really diving into that and, you know, making it the best possible. >> So, where'd your speed come from? Were you a track guy? >> Um, that's actually a funny question. I usually hated track. Um, I didn't really start running track till I was freshman in high school and then, you know, I started winning some medals and was like, you know, I could really do this. Um, but yeah, to be fair, I really hate running. Um, but I'm really good at it. >> 100. Yeah, 100. I was a two-time state champ in the 100. Two time state champ. Um, and then whatever relay my high school needed me to to be a part of that we can make it to state. And so, um, yeah, I take pride in that. >> Have Q or lad given you any advice or encouragement going into your first year and like what are they telling you just to get navigate through this first season? >> Absolutely. Um, you know, I've picked their brains a lot. Um, just kind of, you know, whether it's a certain route or a certain play or just, you know, how do they see these things? And, um, I think they've both been very great, very complimentative, um, of me and what I've been able to do so far. And I, you know, I think the word of them two guys as well along with everybody else in the room, DD, Trey, I think, um, everybody in that room has something that I can pick from and take from. And so I'm not only asking questions of those two guys, but I'm asking questions around the room. Um, just trying to be the best I can be. >> Ke and of course we get linemen in there. We ask him about putting the pads on, but just what about you in terms of putting the pads on and what you might want to show out there? >> Um, I think it's going to be the exact same. Um, you know, I think pads, no pads, I'm going to play the same solid football. Um, I'm going to be aggressive. I'm going to be um you know whatever it takes. I'm still going to run really fast pads or no pads. >> Are there any other receivers past or present that you looked up to or try to emulate when you especially like quick receivers? >> Um I think Tyreek's a little a little in the category just because coach Medino did have Tyreek. Um and I think you know I can be used in some of the similar ways. Um you know Deshawn I think is another Sean Jackson's another one that I kind of look up to. Um, but overall I think I'm a very different receiver than, you know, really what I've seen and what I've, you know, grown up watching. Um, so yeah, I think I'm just going to use my game and my techniques and go out there and be the best I can be. >> Is there anyone on the other side of the ball any DS that you're seeking out advice from? >> Um, yeah, I think DJ, um, I just literally just talked to him after practice today and, you know, we were just talking talking about how, um, you know, when he lines up, he's going to go, you know, harder than he goes maybe versus anybody else. just trying to really prepare me for that moment. Um, I think that's something that, um, is very awesome, um, that we, you know, they have the competitiveness that we have in this locker room and on this team to make each other better. >> [music]

title: Sean McVay, Matthew Stafford & Trent McDuffie Address The Media After Training Camp Practice
text: for for your team. How do you how do you evaluate where you guys are at at this point in the year? >> I think we're just, you know, it's hard to say, you know, like benchmarks or checkpoints. >> Yeah. But, uh, but really, um, I would just say we're just trying to improve every single day as we're kind of adding our installation. We've got the majority of our foundational stuff in. And then we're just kind of adding some situational calls or some different things in different phases that we have, whether that's some different things in the pressure package, whether that's a couple different things in the red area. And so, um, you know, I I thought today was a good step in the right direction. You know, these four day blocks, you know, the first two days represent opportunities to be able to walk through, then practice, then you're more mentally in that third day, and then the last day is, you know, a little bit bigger practice, but we're not doing some [music] of the other mental stuff. And so, I thought the guys handled it well and expect us to come back and continue to build on it in block three. >> What are some of those things that have really impressed you as >> I think just the overall understanding and intent. You know, I think we're looking for guys that can solve problems. There's 22 moving parts every single snap. I think defensively we've got great command on some different things that we're trying to do on really all three levels. I think offensively we're understanding how to solve problems. I think they're positively pushing one another and so that's a positive for us and you know we'll continue to take it a day at a time. >> Know the other day um Cam Curl when describing camp said it's love. >> Yeah. >> Out here I mean the the vibe >> how did he say it? Give me the exact thing he said. >> That's exactly what he said. Said it's love. >> It's love. And I guess, you know, >> that could be taken a lot of different ways. >> Well, the way I took it was that the way you've set this up for players, it's it's a grind, but it's >> Say it again. Say say it's love. >> No, you could say, [laughter] >> but anyway, what is that? >> You got to say it otherwise I'm not answering. [laughter] >> Is that conscious or And has that evolved through your time here or what would you say? Well, I think probably what he's referring to is the workload and kind of our balance in terms of what that rhythm is. I got to give Reggie Scott and his group a ton of credit. And I think what I really appreciate about Reggie is our number one goal is to be able to figure out how do we get the necessary work in and it's got to be hard and there's got to be a good struggle. But how do we make sure that for real growth there's got to be, you know, stress plus rest and then we get that growth from both of those things in combination. That's the way of excellence. Brad Stolberg, it's a good little book. You check it out, Gary. All right. That's love, too. All right. But, uh, but no, and so, but I love these guys. And so, everything that we're doing is I want them to feel like we're in it with them. We're taking care of them. We're going to push them when we're out on the grass. We're going to challenge them mentally, but then we'll give them a chance to be able to recover and turn over so that that growth can occur. And so, I I would imagine that's what he's talking about. But I love Cam Curl. I mean, just his vibe made a great play today. He's doing a lot of amazing things. And I thought it was a huge deal. Obviously, a lot's been made and about some of the new acquisitions with, you know, with Trent, with Jaylen, um, and with Miles on defense, but resigning Cam Curl is a huge deal for us as well. And, um, you know, he's got a great way about himself, got a great influence on his teammates. I love everything he's about, and that's love. At what point do did during your coaching career did you feel as confident enough that you could maybe take a step back and still have the hard work but not just feel like we're not working hard enough and we're not just constantly grinding out? >> You know, I think I've heard it said before, you don't want to mistake activity for achievement, you know, and so you always want to make sure that you're moving forward and that we're getting something out of it. And I think what's great is is that, you know, when you get equity with these guys, they know that, hey, it is not going to be easy. It's going to be hard, but it's going to be worth it. the struggle is what makes it enjoyable and significant uh when you're doing something that includes a mastery but it also matters and so um you know I don't know if there was a specific point but I think what you really do is you try to pay attention and I've always been you know trying to be as efficient as possible we have not I but we have always tried to be as efficient as possible I think when you give people respect of their time they give it back to you whether that's in the meetings whether that's out here you know we want to get our work in but we also want to respect people's times and make sure that we're cognizant of what's the best way to be able to have that growth reflected and um you know I've been really fortunate Sarah to have somebody like Reggie that's helped educate and and we've been together and we've always been in lock step going into year 10 now and it's a real edge for our group. >> Yesterday Yesterday Devonte said something about that he needs to be told to take a day off because you know he's always going to come out and he said this is the first training camp he's ever had with planned days of restster. What were those conversations like with him knowing that, you know, he can be still a wide receiver too and could have been wide receiver one on other teams? >> Sure. >> What are those? >> Oh, yeah. I mean, we look at it as we got two two ones. Um, and we're fortunate that that we've got both of those guys. But what I would say is is Devonte's leadership's been great. That's really with all of our players. You'd much rather we've got to pull them back and protect them from them because they just want to work. They want to grind. That's been consistent with all of our players. But then you want to be able to explain the thought process behind it ultimately to get that buy in so that we're aligned and um he's been outstanding. Made a couple great plays out here. He's always going to have his presence and um love what he's about and love the fact that we have to do that with him and the rest of our guys because they all want to be out here every single day. >> Matthew um had the production last year, but they didn't get most of training camp together. I know no one will ever use it as an excuse, but can you explain what they were missing by not getting that time and how different it will be now that they've had this time? >> I think time when you're as intentional as they are, Sarah. Just, you know, repetition ends up being the mother of learning, it's also the best way to be able to develop rapport with each other. And that's so important whether you're a center playing with a guard, a guard playing with a tackle or, you know, quarterbacks and receivers. And so, um, I think they really hit their stride. You know, I think what was an easy, you know, kind of identifying, you know, kind of a turning point, if you will, was that Jacksonville game and I thought they had a really good connection and then Devonte had to miss some games and then he obviously made a huge impact in the playoffs. Um, but it's big, you know, if you got two guys that five years from when they finished, they're going to be putting gold jackets on and so I feel really fortunate to be coaching these guys. They love football. They're always really trying to challenge each other. And sometimes I like just being a fly on the wall because I think the player led teams are the best teams and that's what we're in the midst of building right now. >> Because Setson's getting more reps. How do you assess how where he's at now as opposed to even a year ago? Yeah. >> And you got you got to love how he looks. Love again. >> Yeah, he's There you go. He's doing great. I mean, he's he really has, you know, and I've mentioned it. You guys have asked me about this and really with that room as a whole. Dave Reon does a great job. Obviously, Matt Matthews leadership. Um, but he's really just taking advantage of his reps and and he's aggressive. You know, he's a playmaker. You know, he's going to he's going to be aggressive but not reckless. He can make some things happen off schedule. The way that we're able to get in and out of the huddle in terms of just his overall command has been in, you know, significantly improved upon. and the way that he works at it. You know, what I did see last year every day is he might not have gotten reps similar to Tai today, but he's walking the field with David going and he's going through the script um as if he's taking those reps on air uh and trying to make sure that he can get better even if it's in the absence of some of the physical repetitions and uh it's cool to be able to see a lot of the work that he's put in, you know, paying off with the way that he's playing and the respect he's got from his teammates. Coach, some of the marquee names that you guys acquired in the offseason, Trent McDuffy, Jaylen Brown, Miles Garrett, they've dominated the headlines, but behind them, you have guys that are quietly having a good camp. Cam Lamp, Emanuel Corbs, and Dez Juan Johnson. Can you talk to me about what you you're seeing out of them this year? >> Yeah, you you just mentioned it. I mean, Dez has been a guy I thought, you know, transitioning to the outside, he's done an amazing job. Been really pleased with him. Uh Cam Lin is a guy, he's got just a great spirit. you know, he's he's one of those guys that seems to be like he it seems like he's always in the right place at the right time. And then who was the third one you asked me about? Eman's been awesome. You know, when he's tapped in, you know, you look at his his top tier plays. He's got the length. He's got the confidence to be able to come up and challenge guys. He can play visual and off. Um I've been really impressed with him. Jimmy Lake has done a great job with our back end. Him and Coach Beak and Mike Hunter. Um you can really see our back end as a whole, but but Eman Dez and Cam Lamin, all those guys have done really nice jobs. Glad you pointed them out. Last year, Stson played first two preseason games because Jimmy and Matthew didn't. Have you made a decision? Can you share how you will handle the quarterback? >> I I haven't decided that yet, you know. I'll I'll uh I'll share that with you guys once we get a little bit closer. We're going to kind of just what's good for me and what I try to really do is just kind of take it one day at a time, you know, because you want to see how did today's practice go. Are we ready to move forward with our installations? Um I don't even know when the first preseason game is. It should be coming up here pretty quickly, but we have an idea of the guys that won't play as far as the quarterback position. Haven't decided on that yet, >> but Matthew won't play. [laughter] >> All right. >> Um, just one last question if you have the time. You mentioned player le teams as well as maybe some unsung heroes of this camp. With so many players returning from last year as well as a few notable additions, are there any players that you think have really stepped up either in new or uh returning to the roles that they had last year? Well, I think what you're seeing is a lot of guys, you know, the veteran, the normal cast of characters, those guys have done a really great job, but I think you're seeing, you know, some of these secondyear guys get more comfortable. Terren Ferguson and Josiah Stewart, you felt their presence. I think Blake Quorm's only getting better and better. Um, you know, but I I could go on and on. I mean, I really love the makeup of this group. And I think the best part of the team is the team, you know, and the humility that our guys have, but they also understand we've got to earn it every single day. Um, but I've been really pleased with a lot of guys. We've got a lot of continuity [music] on the offensive side of the ball. Um, I think David Questberry did a really nice job stepping in playing left tackle. All Alaric, you know, consistent with kind of last week in the block where he missed with taking his medicine. Obviously, uh, love getting out here, being able to compete on the field, but even the moments in the meeting rooms and and the meal rooms with the guys, just being able to, you know, get to know your teammates, and then obviously, uh, you know, install our offense and our defense and our special teams and figure out kind of what we want to be about as a team. So, it's been good. >> Matthew, obviously last year you had the incredible season winning the MVP going into year 18. Yeah, I mean I think just a lot of appreciation for the opportunity, you know, at this point in my career and in my life, my age, um I'm just appreciative to have the opportunity to continue to play. Um I was, you know, blessed to have a great season last year, surrounded by a ton of great players that made great plays for me. Um luckily, uh a lot of those same faces are still out here and they're doing everything they can to try to be as good as players as they can. That's my goal, too, right? I [cheering] I can't sit here and and think about trying to do exactly what we did last year, do it again, you know, from a personal standpoint. I'm just trying to play good football, be the best quarterback for this team that I can be. And if I do that, um, you know, I think, uh, we'll be where we want to be. >> Matthew Co, uh, mentioned or sorry, KO mentioned that Coleman is kind of like the QB2 within your offense, one of those returning pieces. Just how would you describe his role, especially in that MVPC? >> Oh, he's vital. He's vital. um his ability to communicate um in loud environments what we want to get done, you know, quickly, concisely, and clearly for all those guys up front was integral in how well we played both in the run game and the pass game. Um setting the fronts quickly. Here we go. Um let's push the tempo and and uh you the only way you can do that is if everybody's aligned up front. and uh he does such a great job of communicating and spreading that word down the line of scrimmage for those guys so they can play with a quiet mind and play fast and physical. [cheering] >> Devonte uh speaking the other day said on the plane ride [crying] after the loss to the Seahawks in the NFC Championship game, you were sitting in front of him and turned around and said, you know, sorry we couldn't get that done. Yeah. >> What what do you remember that and what precipitated, you know, you saying that to him? >> Yeah. I mean, he's just a a great player, a great teammate, um a guy that um has accomplished a lot obviously on a on a personal level in this league and been a part of some really good teams that just haven't gotten the opportunity to go get that done. And and so just as much as, you know, I wanted to go play in that game, um and a lot of other guys did too, I mean, I wanted it more for other guys that haven't either gotten the opportunity to be there or win it. And uh so just one of those moments where reflecting as the season ends um you know just one of the few things one of the only things we missed out on was the opportunity to go play in that game and so um just on my heart at the moment and decided to tell him how I was feeling. Matthew, we both have the same back doctor. So, I'm wondering when the uh when the long flight comes. Has there been any have you talked to Kersh at all about his few long flights? But you did have a you did have a horrendous year after one bad fight. >> Yeah, thanks. You know, thanks. We're trying to help. >> I don't know if this is wood, but uh >> my head is >> No. Yeah, exactly. No, I uh No, there's there's obviously challenges to playing that that far away from home. Yeah. >> Um and doing it um you know, after a long flight. There's no question about that. I'm sure we'll come up with a great plan. Uh I'm sure they'll have me moving around on that plane more than I want to, but uh I think we'll be all right. >> Have you talked to Curse at all about that? >> I have not. Um but maybe I will. >> Might be a good call. >> Said that one NFL season is like seven like dog years. So that would make him 91. [laughter] >> Do you agree with that? And what would that make? >> Yeah, sometime. Yeah, they're still counting how old I [clears throat] am. But um [laughter] >> no, uh yeah, I'm with them. you know, they it takes a lot out of you. You know, people it's not even the physical part of it for me. A lot of times it's just the mental and emotional part out of it. You know, we sit there and you know, yeah, there's oh, you played with this injury or that injury and those things heal and and so do the emotional things, but at the same time, it just to go week in and week out and put yourself out there and, you know, not knowing obviously what the results going to be. You go line up in Seattle in the NFC Championship game against the best team in the league last year. They won the Super Bowl at their place. 90,000 people screaming at you, man. It takes a lot out of you to try to go just give it everything you possibly have. And and um week in and week in, week in and week out, year in and year out, it takes a lot out of you. And so I understand what he's saying. Um but he still looks good to me. So he's still moving around good. [laughter] >> Matthew, you've talked about how you guys are working on raising your floor. It's an offense out here. What does that look like to you and are you seeing some of that so far? Yeah, I mean I think um you know you're not always going to throw every ball perfect and or catch every ball or or um you know hit every block perfect. All those things those things are going to happen. You're going to have turnovers. You're going to have you know incompletions and bad series bad plays. Just how to you you know reset and and continue to move forward. And I think that's something that you continue to build out here. This is the perfect example of it, right? We make a big play, we don't move the ball down there. It's okay, move it all the way back and you know on the next play. vice versa, the defense makes a great play, you know, well, it's still our ball the next play and we just keep moving. So, it's just how do you move on to the next play and that's an like a mental and emotional thing that you can train and continue to get better at. And so, I think we do that whether it was a, you know, a gain of 50 on a pass play or a run of minus two. How do we reset and move forward? And and that's something that, you know, this practice field is a good thing to to train yourself on. >> Matthew, it feels like a really good day on both sides of the ball for you guys. What's really impressed you about what you guys have done so far up to this point? >> Yeah, exactly what you said. But I think just the quality of football. Um, you know, there was a a lot of high quality plays out there, plays that, you know, in the books will go down as good for the offense and in the books it'll go down as good for the defense that sometimes you just tip your cap, you know? I mean, they covered a couple things really nicely and and were plays where maybe in a game they they shake out a little bit different, we go to the ground or whatever it is, but like, man, that's that's as high quality of practice football as I've been around. And so, that part of it is really fun. and and uh we're stressing ourselves physically making those plays, but also mentally like making sure that, you know, our defense has given us a bunch of different looks. Hopefully, our defense feels like we're giving them a bunch of different looks on offense. So, it's fun to come out here and compete. I don't take it for granted to get out here and and practice against and with a bunch of great players. >> What have you learned about Trent McDuffy going against him now? >> Yeah, I mean, just uh relentless competitor, ultra ultra competitive guy that um play in and play out is where he's supposed to be. Um, does he make a play on it every single time? Absolutely not. But man, he's in a he's giving himself a chance, you know, them because Devonte was saying the other day, we were asking him about you and he just kind of paused says, "I don't I don't want to set this up and make this >> but and then he did. You're just different." And he said, "Going against you is just really different when you're across the line." >> Yeah. you're looking across at him as a guy I'm sure you watched even before you got in the league tearing it up. What's your mindset when you're lined up opposite Devonte? >> I mean, it's a lot of respect. You know what I mean? Knowing who you're going to go against, knowing the type of player he is, and knowing that every rep he gives you is going to be 100%. And that's what I love. Like, that's when I first came here, knowing who I was going to practice against. Um, I was excited because they're just going to get me better. Like that's really what this is all about is just how much can you keep stacking days in order to achieve your goal at the end of the day and going against guys like Devonte who is the best route runner in the league who has the best release is like yeah he going to beat me a lot of the times because I'm trying new things just like he's probably going to try new things and the more we can just keep ping ponging back and forth against each other and the more we can just keep rising our standard um it's going to be a great year for both of us. So I enjoy it a lot. Football is football, but how do you assess what's different between what you guys did at Kansas City and what you're doing now from a training camp standpoint that stands out to you? >> Yeah. Um, I think the biggest thing just over here is the recovery time they like to get, you know. Um, I think that's really big, especially now in training camp where it's longer days. We're out here practicing hard. Um, to just give yourself a second to recover your body, recover your mind. And um my favorite thing about that has been like the DBs get together and play games. We were playing cards the other night and just really getting to know each other, which I think is a very big aspect of being a great team, um is knowing who you're playing with. So, not only are you recovering your body, your mind, and all that, but like we're generally spending time with each other, which to me is special, especially being new here. >> Trent, building off your time in Kansas City, obviously you went up against some of the most special offensive minds we've seen. When you look at this offensive group in Los Angeles, what do you think makes them so special? >> I mean, they're a machine, you know what I mean? Stafford's back there. One, two, three, balls out. He's no looking. Like, Puka's running Chris routes, Devonte's out there. I mean, they got three tight ends that can all get down the field. Um, and it's just a very unique offense that I haven't seen a lot in my career, which I've enjoyed playing against. Um, but they're just a group that can do a little bit everything, you know what I mean? They got two running backs, Karen and Blake, that can both catch the ball, run the ball. The O line's great. Like, I think this offense is going to make our defense even that much better. Just being able to line up against them and have the struggles of just what they do that's so unique with Shawn McVey. >> I know the sample size isn't huge yet, but obviously, how do you think that offense has made you a better player? >> Like I said, just the different looks, you know? Um, I gotta go line up against T Ferg and Higs, and I gota go line up against Devonte and Puka. like you're seeing a lot of different looks, doing a lot of different things the same way, different ways, and um it's all all comes back to your technique and your discipline. >> Trent, I know that number 22's always been close to your heart. So, what did it mean to you to come to a new team and be able to get that number and and for Blake Coron to be willing to give it up to >> Yeah, I mean, shout out Blake. He was um really cool about it. You know, I reached out and he was already like, "It's going to be your number. Like, it's all good." Which I can appreciate. you know, you always hear all these crazy stories this, that, and third. But, um, Blake's one of those guys that is down to earth that's truly special, man, of God. And, um, yeah, I'm just thankful that I'm able to get back the number and kind of just knowing what it represents to me and what I'm going to be, um, on that field and how I can represent it. So, um, appreciate you, Blake. >> Cam Curl was Cam Curl was talking about how the way Sean structured practice and I know you mentioned it with the recovery time. Do you feel that it's you work hard when you're out there, but you get it's it's not maybe as hard as some of the other as where you were in Kansas City. Is it different? >> It's different. I mean, it's still hard. You know what I mean? Especially when you come out here to practice and guys are really giving it their all. Um, like I said, I think the biggest thing is just he allows you to kind of give yourself that that mental space to kind of unload and get away from football for a minor second. And not in the sense of like we're going to just leave and go do our own thing, but um like we practice and we don't have meetings afterwards. It's come get your recovery, eat, spend time with the guys. And I think that's really cool just as a team bonding aspect of how they do things around here. >> Did you take Blake out to dinner? >> Say it again. >> Did you take Blake out to dinner? I haven't yet, but I'm going to get him some before season start. I already told him, >> you only as strong as your weakest link. Can you talk to me about Cam Lin and uh Eman? >> Yeah. I mean, they're ballers, you know what I mean? And each day, my favorite part about them is they want to get better, you know what I mean? They're taking notes in meetings. They're out here applying what we did in the classroom to the field. Like me and L were talking about Nickel today, and I watched him three reps in a row do exactly what I told him. And even though it might have not been perfect, like you can see him trying. you see Eman confidence building like I think just being around guys that trust you you know guys that are going to build you up there's not a single ego on this team that I have come across um it gives you this special place to want to get better and want to get better not only for yourself but for the guys around you know what I mean like me wanting to get better for our offense and for the guys next to me is the same way E and L want to get better to make sure that when their time comes if it ever comes they're ready to step in that role and produce >> thanks Thanks for signing

text: The offense, are you seeing them coming more and more competitive and that's what a lot of people hope to see with the offense and the defense having that back-and-forth? >> Uh I feel like just being here is going to be competitive. I mean, I feel like he has that same mentality we have, you know, on the defense and uh shucks, I'm excited. >> What have you noticed with CJ from last off-season into so far this off-season for him? >> Uh I feel like CJ CJ is definitely commanding more from the offense as a whole, I feel like. I feel like, you know, every year I've seen him, he's always commanded a lot, but this year I feel like he's putting more of that weight on his shoulders, and I feel like it's really good, you know. Chidobe, the new rookie in our corner room. He's really good player. He comes in every day. He's super talented. You I mean, you want me to just name the whole secondary? I think everybody's I'm going to name everybody, you know. title: How Texans RB1 David Montgomery is 'already a team leader' and much more on state of team at camp
text: Hey guys, Aaron Wilson. One of the big changes to the Texans, a dramatic change, is the running game. And the arrival of David Montgomery via trade from the Detroit Lions could dramatically change the whole tenor and mentality of the offense. And I think it already is. It's only one week into training camp, and what I see from Montgomery is leadership, toughness, and a little more wiggle than maybe some people thought he had in the open field. He's down to 225 lb, tells me he's in the best shape of his life. And I'm seeing that paid dividends with how quick he is out of the backfield, and all the things he can do as a runner. He's got good vision, he's got a nose for the end zone, and he definitely has a lot of gas left in the tank because he split carries with Jamaal Williams with the Lions. That ultimately led to his wanting to be a bell cow, RB1, whatever you want to call it, but he's the primary running back. And yes, he's going to see a ton of action. And seeing Montgomery and how he's fit into the locker room, and how he's fit in the offense, the framework of the Nick Caserio system, it's been really instructive to watch that. So, thinking about David and just the type of player he is, he's off to a great start. But I've watched him, the momentum, the acceleration, the power, it's all been on display. And just wait until the pads come on on Monday when you can see him run through and truck some guys. And that's why they call him Knuckles. They don't give you the nickname like Knuckles if you're not tough, obviously. And you know, you've seen that he can lower the boom, but he's also shown that he's got some speed. And the tandem he's formed with Dameon Pierce, I think it'll be really strong. So, they signed him to a two-year $16.5 million deal after he joined the Texans. So, there's going to be pass-catching duties, there's going to be as you know, I talked about this before, Danny Barrett, the running backs coach and assistant head coach told me three down back can do it all. So, featured role after complimenting Gibbs. And in talking with David, this is something he really embraces is the leadership mantle that he's taking on. the mentality and what he wants to do to put a a real imprint and his impact, his signature onto the offense, but the you know, desire to leave a mark on the game, help the younger guys, develop a mindset. Last year, just in a complimentary role, 716 yards, eight touchdowns. This year, I think he's going to rush for over 1,000 yards and 10 touchdowns. He's 5'11, he's 225 lbs. title: Reunited! Jadeveon Clowney exclusive. Back with Texans: 'Chasing Super Bowl'
text: Hey guys, an official reunion between the Texans and former top overall pick Jadeveon Clowney. Three-time Pro Bowl pass rusher rejoins the Texans on a one-year deal with a maximum value of 8 million and a base value of 5.5 million. And I exclusively spoke with Jadeveon Clowney. He told me it wasn't about the money, it was about chasing a Super Bowl and about his legacy. He wanted to have this full circle moment. As I reported last week, he wanted the Texans. It was just a matter of whether the Texans would compete with him financially and in terms of the other teams, the Cleveland Browns most prominently and also the Seattle Seahawks. So, they get this deal done. It's exactly what he wanted. He wanted to play for what has now become his hometown. He lives here year-round and trains with Ben Fairchild. And in talking with JD, I'll give you some of the comments. It's a just a phone interview, so I don't have the audio. But let me tell you what he had to say about playing for the Texans and what I think the impact of this move is. He says it's great. It was a family decision. Not about the money, it was about legacy and chasing a Super Bowl. I've got a lot of game left. I want to contribute. He contacted DeMeco Ryans made it his preference to be with the Texans instead of the Cleveland Browns and the Seattle Seahawks. He said he was looking forward to playing for DeMeco. Pretty exciting coach to play for. He said he reached out and told him he wanted to play for him. As I said, full circle moment. Former top overall pick for the Texans. Had some issues there with the microfracture surgery. And then eventually, his knee got healthy enough. He should have probably not played his first season, but he was so excited. He's grown up a lot. He's matured. He's a dad. He has three kids. He's been, you know, just really growing as a player and as a person for years. He's still got something left in the tank, as he told me earlier this offseason. So, I've had a lot of access to JD and watched one of his workouts. I can tell you he's in top shape. He said with this full circle moment, he was so excited. He had other opportunities, but when he found out the Texans were interested, it's is no-brainer. It was comfortable for him to do that. He's excited to help the situation. So, what does it mean for the Texans? Having Clowney as their third defensive end working in tandem with Pro Bowl pass rushers Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter, that makes a formidable top-ranked defense even stronger. Specifically, when asked about Will and Danielle, he said, "I was excited about playing with those guys. Good defense. I can help contribute. A good chance to chase a Super Bowl. I know what it looks like. I can help the squad." Yes, he can. And as I said, he lives here. He had a strong season with the Dallas Cowboys last year, and he's in outstanding condition. He had 8 and 1/2 sacks last season for the Cowboys, and he's still in good condition, and definitely strong and capable of making an impact entering his 13th NFL season. As he told me, he stands on his grind. He's got a lot left in the tank. He said he doesn't know if other people know that, but he knows that he can continue to prove that to people and go out there and show people he's going to do that. And I think he proved his point last year. He only played 44% of the overall defensive snaps, but he had 8 and 1/2 sacks, 41 tackles. Sack total is highest since the 9 and 1/2 sack, 19 quarterback hit year in 2023 with the Baltimore Ravens. Last season, 12 tackles for losses, 10 quarterback hits. The final game of last season, vintage Clowney, unblockable. Giants offensive line had no answers for Clowney. Six tackles, 2 and 1/2 sacks, one forced fumble, a fumble recovery. He was a menace, just hunting and chasing down Jackson Dart and Devin Singletary all game. And he had said he wanted to go through a full training camp. He's missed just 1 week, but he wanted to have a training camp and have this time. So, it was playing for Dallas last year. It was special for him. And now he's a Texan. So, he's got this background in 4-3 and 3-4 defensive schemes. I think he fits the 4-3 just perfectly, this style of defense. So, when you think about what he can do, and he says, "There ain't no scheme he can't play in." He said he can dominate in those schemes and play at a high level. He said he comes off a great season. I agree with him. In limited action, it's certainly great. He wants to prove to people and he just, you know, he's available, walking every year, show people wrong, and prove he can still play at that high level. So, highly motivated, and he just wanted to get it going. Uh yeah, he had a tough start to his career when they drafted him out of South Carolina, and he was an unsigned franchise player, unable to reach an agreement with the Texans. They'd offered him under Brian Gaine's leadership, and ultimately they traded him to the Seattle Seahawks. And I I would say at that point him and Bill O'Brien were not necessarily in a great place, but that was the old days. This is 2026. Texans uh got a third-round pick and Barkevious Mingo and Jacob Martin in exchange for Clowney. So, not great return, but they got something. 18 and 1/2 sacks his final two seasons combined in Houston, and playing for them, he has some positive memories. He said, "It was an experience. He was young. He didn't know anything. Got hurt his first game. Shouldn't have probably played. He listened to the noise in the locker room when he said he ended up having a longer rehab. That affected his career." But he still managed. He's a survivor. Look at the perseverance, the way that he's taken care of himself, the way he's still playing. And you know, guys that took him under their wing, like Whitney Mercilus, and you know, just being a pro, and he's had a long career. So, you know, he says he doesn't care what anybody thinks, but he knows he can play at a high level, and all my conversations with him have been good ones. Uh you know, looking at everything he's done, there's some good metrics. I know that I'm talking to Ben Fairchild, uh the trainer, does a great job. He's worked before with lots of guys, including J.J. Watt and a lot of baseball players. But he says, you know, look at his performance and his health, and he's been very healthy over the last 5 years, and that he would benefit from this. But you look at the performance analysis, sacks to sacks snaps to sacks ratio, rather. So, through the lens of sacks pressure high hurries, it's pretty illuminating. Four sacks per 100 pass rush snaps last season in terms of percentage. title: Jonas Sanker talks role in year 2 | Saints Training Camp 2026
text: Yeah, feels good in here. >> [laughter] >> It's next level. >> Yeah. >> So, I know you've been you've already had a little bit of time to acclimate to the new world and the camp OTAs, but how is it different here in training camp and how do you feel like it's been a good fit for you so far? >> Um, I wouldn't say it's too different in training camp, you know, like you said having OTAs has been really good just, you know, helping me get acclimated, but um, having played so much safety last year, I think there's so many similarities that I could think it makes the transition a lot smoother. Um, coach TJ, coach Daley have all done a great job just, you know, coach RJ as well just helping me, you know, adjust and just kind of tune up some of those little things, but um, I think the biggest thing that's really helped me get comfortable is just you know, the amount of talent we have on the offense that's just giving me tough looks every day. And, you know, through those mistakes and you know, sometimes I get beat, sometimes, you know, I make the play, so I think through all that it's just helped me, you know, learn so much and grow each and every day. >> Did you have an example of that just yesterday? I've worked with some of the corners, just you know, you know, picking their brains, you know, how they're, you know, able to stay square so well and you know, I think Quincy, Ike, Kool-Aid, MJ, all those guys, they do a great job of that. Um but you know, also just, you know, being a rookie, you know, I was able to, you know, be with Alontae, spend so much time with Alontae on the field especially. Um so kind of just seeing how he did a lot of things, whether it's disguising, whether it's, you know, how he played man in different situations. So, you know, I learned a lot just even just watching him. So. >> Did you watch kind of like the Jalen Ramsey, Derwin James stuff in this defense and just kind of see how they do it? >> No, for sure. You you know, I I watch a lot of guys and just see, you know, it's hard for me to kind of just try to emulate my game after one person just because I think everyone's different and you know, especially someone like Jalen Ramsey, you know, he's got such a unique skill set that it's hard to kind of try to play like somebody. So, really just figuring out, you know, how my skill set can be used in my, you know, the best of my ability. So. Um yeah, still kind of learning that and I think you you kind of learn something new every day, but yeah, just kind of getting comfortable. >> And uh Justin Reid was telling us about how like in his rookie year or second year, he dropped down and played some slot too. >> Mhm. Yeah. >> Um like just having that resource there, you know, somebody who's done that, uh how helpful is >> Yeah, no. Justin Reid played some nickel. Um so he has inside, you know, Julian Blackmon played some nickel as well. Um Terrell Burgess, you know, he's played safety and nickel and he's played nickel in Coach Daly's defense as well. So, you know, all those guys know what they're talking about, know what they're doing. It's been great. >> I'm going to stick with you and mention Alontae and all things that make you better, but to back to Justin, I guess he took you under his wing immediately. Can you just paint a picture of that relationship? >> Yeah. No, I mean, he he took me in and, you know, taught me kind of the ways he watches film, you know, the way he, you know, approaches game days, just everything. But you know, I I can't even give him all the credit because, you know, I feel like everyone in my room has been such a great mentor, you know, given that we have so many older guys. Um you know, to me and Elliott, you know, who was a rookie with me as well, you You they kind of took us both in and just really taught us everything they know and have never had like a you know, arrogant approach to the way they do things. They've never felt like they had to keep stuff from us because, you know, they didn't want us to try to you know, outplay them or anything. It was just always so humble and always just caring about, you know, other people, which has been great. >> What did uh Julian mean to you last year? Obviously, he was in that role before you were in it and then the injury happened. >> Yeah, no, I think Julian is really special and I think, you know, having him this year is going to just had a huge make a huge difference just because I think his ability to just, you know, make plays on the ball and just create turnovers, I think is, you know, it's hard to find and I think he's every any You put him anywhere on the field, it doesn't really matter. I think he's just always finds his way to the ball. I mean, you see it, he already has an interception early in camp, so that's just who he is. >> Having a full off-season with the Saints for Julian, how much do you see that as an advantage for him? >> Yeah, definitely, for sure. And even just last year being around, just learning it still. Um, you know, he's not coming into this being new to the defense. He's coming in, you know, being a veteran and having a good having a good grasp on, you know, all the different aspects of the defense. >> When while safety and and corner sometimes are kind of like more field boundary specific, in your role, you kind of have to move and play both sides, right? >> Yeah, no, you Yeah, no, I mean, it's I wouldn't even call it a challenge, you know, you just as long as you're clued in, you know, understanding that, you know, you've got to match not always, but sometimes you've got to match the passing strength, you know, follow the slot receiver around a little bit and it can vary, you know, some some games, you know, we might not feel the need to do it. Some games we might feel the need that we always want, you know, the star traveling to the passing strength, so it's just kind of something you got to be clued in on. >> Just outside of even the coverage stuff, but just being closer to the line of scrimmage, like what's kind of the most important part of it? >> Yeah, no, that was definitely that was definitely, you know, a different challenge for me given that I, you know, I didn't hadn't played much nickel since like freshman, sophomore year of college. Um, but it's It's good, you know, it forces you to kind of make decisions quicker. So, you know, I'm kind of getting a feel on, you know, how I want to line. Do I want to be, you know, 5 yd, 6 yd? Just different situations. So, um it's been really good. You know, that's why we have camp. That's why we we have OTAs. And, you know, I know I'll be ready. >> Does the Does the space that you are accustomed to playing in at safety help you manage the space when you're on the inside? >> Um yeah, I think it it helps in ways. And I think there's a lot of times, you know, at safety when you're to come down, you know, and be a flat player. And, you know, get your be down at six, you know, maybe five yards even. But, um yeah, there's the there's different situations. But, I think at the end of the day, I think safety is is just a different approach in terms of just being more patient and understanding that you are the last line of defense. Whereas at nickel, you know, there's a little more room, you know, for air because, you know, let's say you fit on the wrong side of your man. You know, the safety behind you has got to make you right. And that was kind of, you know, what I was learning last year as a safety. And now, you know, being in that other role, I understand like, okay, I know my safety's expecting to fit here. Let me not screw him over and go the wrong way. So, it's good. >> Thank you. Thank you. >> Appreciate it, both.

Um and that's a different game. That's honestly a different game. And then uh when you're actually playing, it's kind of like you got to switch on, okay, this is what the coaches see. Why would they be calling what they're calling? And then how can I affect this play? Um and so, I feel like mentally I'm very locked in, which I got to be. You know, I think everybody knows that. It's a It's another prove a year. It's another, you know, one-year contract and it's another chance for me to get out there and play a full season. Well, I I I think that I just think of my teammates. Um you know, we had a lot of conversations when I was in Indianapolis with with Ballard GM and you know, that was one of those things where I just wanted to be out there with the guys because I knew that my effect communication-wise was very effective. Um we had a lot of guys that were younger in the room. I think that's something that I'm very good at. Um and so, just being back there kind of hopefully will will tell the quarterback, "Okay, I got to really think about where he's at." >> Did that coaches have any opinion or is that something you're interested in post-career? >> We'll see, man. I mean, maybe younger kids, you know, I I to start out. I feel like I'm more of like a trainer, more of one-on-one person as it is. So, maybe. >> Do you have any guys in Do you have any guys that are, you know, former players one-on-one that you that you worked with like from the opposite side as a player now? No, not No, not anybody right now. No. >> Your With your past history of shoulder injuries, like did that Did that like alert you something was wrong last year like tell me something? >> Look, I don't I don't know. I know it's not the same injury or did it Was it just like, "Damn, my shoulder hurts." >> It's almost like you don't know until you get another surgery, which is funny. Um I felt like after my second surgery coming back this year, it my shoulder felt a lot different than my first one. Um just in terms of how fast I was able to come back and just feeling a lot more comfortable moving it in certain positions that I wasn't able to do last year. Um so it was it was one of those things where I didn't really know how much better it could get until the second surgery. >> Do you know what happened? >> It was the same shoulder, but different different spot. Yeah. >> Do you know what happened on the field that led to it? Like that what caused it? >> I don't know, but I mean there was a couple plays at the end where I mean there was a second down. So I I could I could say that that was probably one of the plays that jarred it a little loose, but like I said, I woke up the next day and that's when I kind of knew that something was wrong. >> Is that a is is that impact recovery at all to not necessarily know exactly how it happened or is like that >> Not really because I mean these days doctors are so good at, you know, pinpointing the injury and how you get it stronger. Cool. Thank you guys. >> Appreciate it, buddy. Good to see you.

title: Saints P Ryan Wright discusses Morstead, nuances of punting, transitioning from QB & more
text: I think that my strengths come from directional punting. I think it makes it a little bit easier on the gunners and I like to I think that I match with my distance and hang time which is a very important part of punting. And things I want to work on a little bit are just the consistency on those going in punts on what exactly yard line I want to hit this ball to now. More often than not I'd say 95% of time it's going to be inside the 20 but just kind of honing in on the range where I want to hit it to 10 to 12 to give myself a little more room for error. >> Is net punting a big concern of yours? >> No. >> Okay. You you had a 73-yard against the Bills. >> Let me Let me Let me ask you what you mean Sorry. What do you mean by big concern? >> Well, it's something that a consideration or something that you would focus on. >> I mean net punting is the most important statistical measure for a punter. Now am I thinking about what exactly that punt >> No, no, I didn't mean that. >> Yeah, I Obviously a punter wants to have anything above a 43 net on average and that's seen as a success. Obviously you're going to get those 50-plus nets and sometimes those going in punts you can't get that much yardage. So but yeah, if you're asking me like if that's the most important statistical measure to absolutely play am I thinking about it rep to rep? No. >> You you had a 73-yard against the Dolphins and I think an 87 against the Eagles if I got the numbers right. Was that one of those games that you just needed a big punt and then the ball rolled away after? >> Um well, actually yeah, both both those punts came in huge crucial spots in the game. A funny story that that Dolphins punt was my rookie year but that was almost a recipe for disaster. I I think I've said this in our story way back then but I was lined up wrong. No, I think I was lined up too deep. I caught it and if you look at the the video a little bit I'm actually rotating the ball as it's dropped to get it the into position. It just happened to connect and know, thankfully it worked out. >> You looked good out there, too. you averaged >> It depends on the route, I'm sure. Yeah. Like I obviously I'm not Like you're a punter's not going to get a 5.5 second hang time, but what I meant earlier about distance and hang time at the same time, if I hit a 45 yard ball, I want to have at least 4.5 seconds of hang time. If I hit a 50 yard ball, I want to have 5 seconds of hang time. If that hang time is lower than that distance, I'm I'm kicking my couch. >> You're a special teams player, but do you think of yourself as a defender? >> It's If it gets to me, yeah. But my goal is to not let the returner get back to me. Otherwise, if I that happens, I didn't do my job. Uh actually in preseason on block field. In preseason, that's that's a good question. >> And when you when you want to you talk about, you know, kind of figuring out your landmarks for where you're trying to go for the direction, how much of that is a call from the sideline and how much is it you get out there and you see how the coverage is aligned and you're quick to figure that out on the field? >> Throughout [snorts] my career, it's kind of been up to me obviously in certain situations. My past coordinator wanted me to hit a certain way and then we discuss it a little bit if I have third down. It sounds like it's going to be pretty much the same, but me and Phil have been on the same page with what we want to do, our goals of direction, distance, and what we actually want to accomplish on each play. Like if you see something like that where a guy's cheating over, is that kind of fitting your realm to be like, "Okay, that's not fair. He's just going to block me." >> Uh yeah, with with precaution obviously cuz if it's a dangerous returner like the term can stand Sleeper Raymond, you do not want to hit that ball to him cuz they already could take that to the house, right? With that low hang time if they get to it is very dangerous. >> How easy when you work with a guy like like that? >> He's doing it better. >> Quality guy. I uh I've gotten pretty close to Zay Jones these last few weeks and uh even leading into OTA's and uh spring ball and he's he just works his ass off every day. He speaks my language. Um but he uh he just one of those pros. Like he's a true vet and I look up to him and I want to try to take everything I can from him. >> Why would you call that a >> I'm playing it too late. >> Did you miss your first Louisiana heat at training camp? >> Can I say yes? >> That's a that's a answer. I don't know if >> No, I didn't even I I I'm I'm still getting used to the heat a little bit. Um I'll get there. I'll get there. I definitely like this over the -20 wind chill. >> That's a fact. >> I don't know if it was your biggest one, but it came against the Saints. >> Um can you just speak to that that play and the irony that that play came against this team? >> Yeah, I mean it's very ironic. Obviously, it was a really cool play, very cool experience. My first NFL completion and it happened to be in London, too. And uh now looking back, I know I'm on the Saints now and I was like, "Shoot, why did I do that?" But uh now hopefully I can bring that same element to to the Saints and we can complete some more passes. >> Is that the only one you have so far? >> So far, yeah. >> So you're one for one then? >> One for two. >> Oh, okay. Yeah, got it. >> Ron, how'd you learn that really quick situation? >> Um so I was a quarterback in high school and um at that point I was more doing punting as a hobby. I was I was working on it, but it was more of a hobby, kind of that second position behind quarterback. And um I was the Colts kicking guy, so Jamie Kohl uh reached out to Tui Latu and Tui Latu is a punter. her. And Willie Fritz gave me a shot and I committed right on the spot. >> What kind of experience was it with Tulane there? >> It was very fun. Obviously I'm from California so a little bit of a culture change but first I mean first year I was a little homesick a little rough but I met my life long friends there and I had a really good time there. >> How do you think the fan base was when you were there and what do you think of the Saints fan base? >> So far they've been great. Fans have been showing up at practice and you know I they're getting loud and it's exciting. I can't wait to hear how loud the game is in the dome. >> Has it been everything you wanted it to be so far and why? you know I I I've come into a come to a team with a lot of great guys and when that happens football's a lot of fun and you know I I think that energy's high, the confidence is high and I think that's going to bleed into the season. >> Playing a quarterback in high school like if I told you in high school you'd be a punter today >> Oh I would thank you're crazy. >> What would you have said then? >> I would think you're crazy. At that point. At that point. >> Did did you have a model of punter as that you kind of modeled your style after or did you just punter your own style? >> Thomas Morstead. >> Really? >> Yes Morstead. >> Yeah. When I I think that was a kind of a combination of who the best punter was at that time when I was starting to transition from quarterback to just being punter and also being here in New Orleans I got to see him work out at Tulane a lot and I think I kind of modeled my short steps after him and I try to be a directional punter like him and I think that it's >> One of the things over the last 10 years changed dramatically >> is been long range field goals, secondly the directional punts. How much work do you do in the off season cuz you you want to know who you're punting to. >> Yes. >> And watching who the return man is but also trying to get a certain direction on your >> Mhm. I mean, I I I've been a directional punter, boundary punter since I was at Tulane. We were the first ones to boundary punt a team. So, I've I kind of came into the NFL with that mindset already.

title: Taliese Fuaga on Physicality in Camp and Developing Callouses
text: I know it's kind of cliche when first day of pads and everything. Like how how does that kind of up everything for you guys if it changes anything at all? >> [snorts] >> Yeah, no. So, the same thing on the opposite side, how do they make y'all better? >> Man, it's just well, you got a little change up like Cam. Cam's been in the league for probably like 50 years now.
