title: Can Jerry Jones save Tony Romo's CBS gig? | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: There's another wrinkle in all of this and that came to light on Saturday when Jerry Jones, the owner and general manager of the Dallas Cowboys, spoke to Fox 4 in Dallas Fort Worth. Jerry Jones loves Tony Romo. That's my quarterback. He had everything but the sunglasses and the crocodile tears. He loves Tony Romo. Tony Romo is a very, very unique talent. Jerry Jones said he's an excellent portrayer of the action. He can see everything. If CBS wants to get rid of Romo, they may have to go through Jerry Jones. And it could be could be that they've already ignored Jones in putting Tony Romo on leave. There's no way that just happened without some sort of advanced conversation and discussion. Maybe not with Romo directly, his agent, somebody from CBS. What are we going to do? This is what we're thinking. Well, we don't want to do that. Well, we want to do it. Somebody calls Jerry. Jerry calls someone. What are you thinking? Putting this very, very unique talent on leave. Like, it's possible the bat signal's already been activated by Tony Romo to get Jerry Jones to intervene. If it hasn't already, it will be. Jones, even without a request from Tony Romo, Jones understands what's going on. And here's the real issue. Does Jerry Jones have the power he used to have when it comes to the networks? Because look, the NFL isn't bashful about micromanaging the networks because the networks are presenting the NFL's product. This is a three-hour infomercial for which the NFL gets paid more than handsomely, and the NFL has a direct say. and who is involved in the infomercial. They want the product to be presented in the best way possible. And that means announcers they like, not personally, but from the standpoint of what kind of a job do they do? How do they present and promote our product on this platform where we are paid billions to have people become further infected by the NFL virus? Big voices, big moments. The feeling I used to get when I was a kid when I knew that Pat Summerall and Tom Brookshshire were calling a game on CBS, that 4:00 game. That was the game to watch by virtue of the fact that Pat Summerall and Tom Brookshshire were calling it because somebody saw fit to put them on that game. That is the game I need to watch today. That's the game to look forward to. And at the Sunday afternoon networks, that's the evidence every week. This is the game that the executives decided is the game. This is the game. And surely there's coordination, communication between the networks that have the full slate of Sunday games and the league as to where they're going to send the top crews. The league will have its opinions on where the the number one broadcast team should be sent, which game is going to send a message to the fans. Most most of the time it's obvious. It only gets tricky when you've got a weekend where, for example, CBS doesn't have the late afternoon game. Fox does. Where do you send Romo and Nance for the one o'clock game? Sometimes it's a surprise where the number one team goes. For the most part, it's obvious, but still, even if it's obvious, it's it feels like a bigger deal. And that explains why there is that involvement. There is that communication. And Jones has always been very influential when it comes to the handling and the managing of the networks. Does he still have that kind of juice? There likely was a time within the past decade where one phone call from Jerry Jones shuts this down. It's a good litmus test because if Romo never comes back to CBS, Jerry Jones is already on record with his opinion and clearly he would disagree with CBS moving on from Tony Romo. So, we've got headline Romo versus CBS, subtext Jones versus CBS. And specifically, what kind of juice does Jerry Jones still have? Can he save Tony Romo's job? He didn't save him from being put on leave. He hasn't prevented this current vibe from taking root. And frankly, the feeling is so widespread that if it's wrong, CBS needs to come out and say, "Whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa. This is temporary. This is temporary. He'll be back." I get the feeling it won't be. Hi, it's Mike Florio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube.

text: Yes. >> Um, I would say the run game has a big factor, especially at the line of scrimmage. It doesn't It doesn't change where the target is. It doesn't change that. title: HC Dan Quinn Speaks To The Media Before Back Together Saturday | Washington Commanders
text: And she was like a warrior and had like unbelievable light about her. So just want to hit you hit them and just let them know we're thinking of them. Want to give a couple injury updates. Trey Burke's will be back at practice today. And John Bates strained his hamstring in Thursday practice. So that'll knock him out for for a couple of weeks. Today's one of our favorite days. We get to share it with the fans and get rolling with that. So we're looking forward to it. A lot of uh third down and end of half situations today for the I talked in the opening time about our block. Today's practice is the end of the first block. And then we'll kind of reassess what we need to hit, what we emphasize again, get into the next one. So let's get rocking with you guys today. >> Um first on the injury stuff, Nick Allegretti? >> Yes, Nick won't be out today. He'll like same thing. He's you know in the next week or so in that space. >> Okay. And then you talked a lot about the energy and getting more in here. What little things have you seen maybe already in this camp that maybe you weren't seeing last year? >> Without looking back too far, I would say I just I don't know if it's compared to last year but I can tell you what I'm seeing now, John. I think like unbelievable connection of the communication back and forth. Not just connection as like a friendship you and I but the work, the communication back and forth together. I saw it in the spring with like Ameer and Mikey just after doing things. And so I'm seeing these pockets of connection and work taking place. And so that would be one example of what I'm seeing. >> DQ, with this defensive front, you guys made a lot of additions in the off season of course and um pretty multiple up there. How does that sort of set the tone for your defense overall? I know obviously the the back end has to do their thing too but you know it tends to start in the trenches. >> Yeah, it does. >> So how does that change it for you guys so far? >> Yeah, we definitely see it starting up front. And different days will emphasize different packages to go. So I think of it as like four down structures. Sometimes it's five like a three four structure. Otherwise sometimes more people up on the line. And so depending on what the offense is doing, it might be heavier or bigger groups. So, I like the versatility of going in and out. Each day you kind of get to work some. Um in other words, in like a a 2-minute or a third down, depending on the distance, might be more spread out and open compared to like a short yardage in that day. So, I like that we have the flexibility to, you know, match different personnel. That's a big deal. >> Dan, uh Jayden Bradley, undrafted free agent, didn't play a lot until his final season at UNLV. First, what made you all comfortable about bringing him in as an undrafted free agent? And then, what has impressed you so far with him in >> Yeah, we also got a chance to visit him um on our local day. And there was a competitiveness that we saw, and um that kind of went through to say, "Okay, through the draft, he he's somebody that's going to be on our space." And so, with Bobby keeping connected with him as it goes, certain times you're like, "Okay, there's a chance after the draft to add somebody with this type of competitiveness." And like, let's face it, if you're going to be undrafted, you better be a dog of a competitor and find your spaces on teams and other spaces. That's what um I've seen from him so far. So, I'm looking forward to to seeing the progress and seeing him develop, um having a hunger to want to improve. Like, that's the first step, and he definitely has that. >> Coach, with the fans being here, does it change how you guys approach practice as far as not showing too much? Or, you know, is there anything of that nature with the fans being here? >> Nope. So, we'll stay along that path to go. But, um big playbook, big things to go. And so, as we're going through it, it's more just us, you know, staying on rhythm and on routine for us, but no change. But, it is nice to have the energy of them here. Sometimes when you're here all the way, you you know, you don't hear them and feel them. And so, it's nice to share the day with them. >> Coach, if this is an incorrect observation, I apologize. But, when you're going ones on ones, it feels like you guys are call uh blowing the whistle a little early, especially when Jayden's escaping the pocket on plays. In games, we might see him make it. What's the rationale for blowing the whistle when you are? >> Not more than normal or less than normal. Um you may see some days where he's outside the pocket, where he stays behind the line of scrimmage, uh as opposed to running it down the field. We have a excellent idea of what that looks like and when he uses that. So, we're when we're extending some plays to go, but also I want it to be, you know, in a true competition sense. In some of them, this was a sack. I'm blowing the whistle. And he can definitely say they wouldn't have got me, and like yes, they probably wouldn't, but like we're doing it anyway. >> And at this point in camp, what's your thoughts on the secondary so far? >> Yeah. Tomorrow we'll get into our first kind of assessments. What do we like about block one? Where are we at? So, as we're going through the installs, a lot of mix of different people. But um the disguises are coming. That's part of, you know, playing the position. We're still seeing different versatility, but it'll be a while. It's not something long that we're thinking with Nick. It does give you a window to see where people are at. More reps, somebody came alive, this happened, and so I like that to see who is here and elevate them and see what that looks like. And often times you're surprised to say, "Hey, okay. You put him in the fire, see where it goes." And like let's let's see where we go from there. >> Again, logistically, um this first pads Tuesday and then Go ahead. >> Monday. >> Monday. Okay. And so we're kind of just working it back and forth. But yeah, it took a lot of time through the spring and through the summer to like absolutely try to nail it. >> It's all designed. >> Yes. >> And when you're installing two new systems, do you structure film study, you know, walk-throughs, practices any differently, giving guys more time here and there? How do you kind of evaluate how they're learning? >> Not more time, but certainly um teach-backs. If you really want to test someone's learning, you have to ask the questions and explain them back to them. Like think of all of us in school, like somebody was teaching or lecturing and like, "Okay, did they take this information in?" And so that's really what we want to do. You think of like crawl, walk, run. The crawl part is like the meetings and then in the evenings, walk-throughs. And then out to practice. So those three steps are a big one. Um we try to put some things in some buckets that mean something. So these T words mean this, these, you know, D words mean this. So we try to find common themes for the teaching. But if you really want to know it, you have to have the the player teach it back to have a real understanding. >> I am not thinking of anybody in particular here, but you guys have a ramp-up procedure when guys are coming in. >> Um if I remember correctly, Noah had been in camp when you brought him in. So, does the fact if somebody's been in a camp, does that change their ramp up and as opposed to somebody that hasn't been? >> Yes, it definitely does. Um reason being it like they've kind of been through some of the football training and also did they go through an off-season program or not? Sometimes that can factor in as well, but if you haven't had the person as part of your program, yeah, I think it makes sense to see where they're at and moving forward. The latest generation has has has BMF on the back. Probably good guess of what that means, but what does it What does it mean and how does it apply to Apply it to this year's >> know what you're referring to. >> this year's like motto or or anything. >> for sure. I think you guys know me well enough. Having an identity for a team is is important and it's not, you know, on a back of a slogan or hung on a wall. It has to be something that's done every day, but standards and identity of what you want to be, it has to be established over time and consistently. And for us, you know, we want our fans and our team and everybody watch us play say, "Man, these guys really bring it." And so, that's what we want to establish, but uh it takes time for that to happen. And uh I'm looking forward to seeing this team. You know, each team there's a new group, a new seeing these guys build it together. Like I'm pumped to see their connection happening quickly already and that's a good sign for a coach. >> Um going back to Barry's question, it does seem like a lot of teams across the league, their approach to training camp in general has changed. Like not more than 3 days in a row for camp. >> And it's not simply because of the changes in the CBA. What has sort of been your view of it and, you know, how have you kind of approached all of it? >> Yep. So, there's definitely some parts of it that are, you know, CBA related and that and organized, but I think it's also good like we now have more information, you know, to know hey, this is when this amount of injuries occur at the beginning, so what can change? And so, you saw like a lot of red zone work early to try and limit. Now, is it foolproof? No. Like obviously, we had John get a hamstring on day two, so like it's not what's, you know, like no matter what this will work, but it's a good guidelines, you know, to stay with that. And if we can keep doing that, you know, we're going to in the end be stronger and better. And so, it's that fine line, you know, you want to walk, you want to be right close to the edge, but you don't want to go over it. And that's the same we measure, you know, what did each guy do on certain day and quite honestly, like you do have to have some really hard days to build some resilience and like knowing like how are you going to be ready to play 60 plays if you only play 15 at practice? So, a little bit more, a little bit more, a little bit more, then back down and go higher again. So, there's a lot of thought that goes to it and I wish it was one size fits all, but it's not. It's just like some of them were learning players as David was referring to earlier, somebody is new or a rookie player in their first camp. So, I think just having an open mindset each night, we discuss it, who might need more, who might need less, what needs tweaking as opposed to well, this is on the script, we should do what it says. So, that's important piece. >> So, a lot of it is sort of based on like league trends, maybe or like medical research, just >> Definitely not media trends. Yeah. >> [laughter] Yeah, but maybe one day. >> Um, but it does and um I think that's important, you know, like it's kind of how we grow the game knowing that like this would be a safer approach for guys to have better health long term.
